newsitem.title: THAILAND: Minister urges Asia to ride out economic slowdowns.
newsitem.headline: Minister urges Asia to ride out economic slowdowns.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Friday urged top corporate executives to sustain Asia's economic miracle by looking beyond the current slowdown in growth in the region.

Amnuay said in a speech to the CEO Forum, a gathering of more than 100 top business executives, that Asian companies could ride out economic slumps by improving efficiency, adopting open-market practices and embracing new technology.
He said the high growth economies of East and Southeast Asia saw economic expansion slow to an average 7.3 percent in 1996 from 8.5 percent a year earlier.

"(The slowdown) has stimulated much speculation about the durability of the so-called Asian miracle... While the Asian growth miracle is certainly not over, we should not rely too much on high rates of expansion to grow our businesses out of trouble.
"We must look more carefully at improving customer service, relying less on protected domestic markets, and at adjusting for both the highs and lows of economic growth cycles."
Amnuay reminded his audience that by 2005, East Asia's share of global gross domestic product could reach a third, up from about 25 percent currently estimated by the World Bank.

Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, in a speech read out to the audience by Amnuay, said Thailand's sharply slowing growth in the past year had forced it to review its fiscal and monetary policies.
Thai economic growth, hurt by weak exports, fell to 6.7 percent in 1996 from 8.6 percent in 1995. Private analysts forecast GDP will expand about five percent this year.

"By mid-1996, we began to get some signals that it was time to go back into the kitchen and rebalance the mix of fiscal and monetary policies and moderate the high-risk, expansionary practices of some institutions in our financial and property sectors," Amnuay quoted Chavalit as saying.
A four-year slump in the Thai property sector has shaken the stability of Thai banks and finance firms saddled with growing piles of non-performing loans.
Chavalit characterised the economic slowdown as an industrial transition which, he said, was accompanied by government determination to push ahead with bureacratic and constitutional reforms.
